source.title: Deep learning generalizes because the parameter-function map is biased towards simple functions
source.authors: Guillermo Valle Pérez; Chico Q. Camargo; A. Louis

record.file_problem: not stated; the supplied text includes the paper and appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports label-corruption experiments and training and generalization errors, bearing on random-label fitting and degradation with label noise. It describes these as replications of Zhang et al. (2017a), but uses its own datasets and experimental setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for binarized MNIST, fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR10 under increasing label corruption, with training set error stated as zero. Figure 3 values across corruption levels are not given in text and are recorded as figure only. The paper cites other studies on regularization, shuffled inputs, training time, and learning simple patterns; those cited results are not rows.
record.test_reason: Section 6 explicitly replicates the label-corruption experiment using SGD and empirical training and generalization error. The binary classification tasks and architectures differ, but the method and measures address V1 and V4 directly.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors propose strong simplicity bias in the parameter-function map as a principal explanation of generalization. Their corruption experiments reproduce increasing generalization error with zero training error, while their PAC-Bayes bounds track that trend. The explanation remains conditional on approximations, especially how closely SGD resembles Bayesian parameter sampling.
record.recipe_differences: The paper reports label-corruption experiments resembling Zhang et al. (2017a), across binarized MNIST, fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR10, using its stated FC and CNN architectures and SGD setup. It does not establish that every original architecture or hyperparameter was unchanged.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and architecture differ in the reported uncorrupted generalization errors; Figure 3 shows separate curves for CNN and FC across three datasets. The paper also states PAC-Bayes bounds depend on variance hyperparameters, but these do not alter the label-corruption outcome rows.

fits_no_version.finding: Figures 13–16 measure iterations to perfect fitting against target-function complexity, but targets were sampled from network parameters and are explicitly described as probably not fully random.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimization effort can vary with Boolean target-function complexity.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix A reports that plain SGD often failed to reach zero error on Boolean-function tasks after many thousands of iterations; advSGD usually succeeded, and Adam required a different loss. The failed targets are not identified specifically as completely random labelings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Perfect fitting of Boolean targets can depend on optimizer and loss choice.

fits_no_version.finding: Parameter-function probabilities, complexity correlations, and PAC-Bayes bounds concern simplicity bias and predicted generalization, without measuring the temporal ordering in V6.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The parameter-function map favors simple functions and can help predict generalization.

record.problems: Exact Figure 3 values across corruption fractions are not stated in the text. The text gives no uncertainty for those curves; empirical errors are averaged over 8 initializations. Results use binarized datasets and a specified training setup, and do not report shuffled or Gaussian inputs or explicit regularizer interventions.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible results were omitted. Figure 3 curve values are retained as figure-only rows; no exact values were reconstructed from the plots.

untested.parts: The exact chance-level test-error endpoint cannot be verified from the supplied figure text. The experiments use their own fixed architectures and training recipe, rather than establishing equivalence to the original source's settings.
No readable random-versus-real-label training-time ratio or convergence-time sweep over corruption fractions.
No fitting experiments with shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
No controlled removal or addition of weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation.
No training trajectories separating acquisition of real-label patterns from memorization of noise.

missing.what: Additional random-target fitting evidence: the authors state that the small Boolean network can fit random functions and that genuinely random targets yield generalization error equal to or above their unbiased learner. Record the optimizer caveats from Appendix A; do not infer a numerical success rate or chance-error value.
missing.locator: Appendix F.4, opening paragraphs; Appendix A; Section 4

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text contains figure captions but no readable plotted curves. Missing numerical endpoints are evidence limitations, not evidence against the claims. Boolean optimizer failures do not establish a challenge to completely random-label fitting because the text does not identify which target functions failed.

versions.untested_parts: Whether test error is at chance for every random-label setting is only shown in Figure 3; exact values at complete corruption are not stated in text.
The text does not provide numerical test errors or uncertainty at each corruption fraction; the trend across fractions is shown in Figure 3.
